Type & translate

Your words, replaced in place.

Works in any app

Browser, Word, Notepad, chat — KBMK lives in your system tray and follows your typing everywhere.

Translations are cached, so a word you have used before comes back immediately — no waiting, no extra requests.

Bring your own provider

Your keys. Your choice.

KBMK translates through a provider you pick, with a key that stays yours. Keep several profiles, test each connection, and watch real usage counters on every one.

Google Cloud

Google Cloud Translation, with the widest language coverage — all 100+ languages, Bengali included.

100+ languages

Microsoft Azure

Microsoft Azure Translator, keyed with your own key and region. A generous free tier, and Bengali is supported.

Key + region

DeepL

DeepL, known for natural European languages. It covers around 35 languages — and does not include Bengali.

~35 languages · no Bengali

There is also an experimental keyless mode if you just want to try KBMK first. And if a key runs out of quota, optional fallback can move to your next key — the pill always announces the switch. It never switches silently.

Private by design

Nothing to sign up for.
Nothing watching.

There is no KBMK account and no KBMK server in the middle. Your words go only to the translation provider you chose, with your own key. Privacy is not a policy here — it is the whole design.

Keys stay in Windows

Your API keys live only in Windows Credential Manager — the same vault Windows itself uses. They are never written into settings files or exports.

Keystrokes never touch disk

What you type is held in memory only, just long enough to translate the word you finished. It is never written to disk, ever.

Password managers blocked

1Password, KeePass, KeePassXC, Bitwarden, LastPass, Dashlane and Enpass are blocked by default — KBMK never listens while you use them.

Your own block list

Block any app you like, picked from your open windows. In a blocked app, KBMK does not capture a single keystroke.

A word of honesty: builds are unsigned, so the first launch asks for one extra click — on Windows, SmartScreen’s More info → Run anyway; on macOS, right-click → Open. It is a one-time step, and it is only because KBMK is a small independent project, not a company.

Questions

Asked, answered.

Yes — KBMK itself is completely free. Translation runs through your own API key (Google, Azure or DeepL), and those providers offer generous free tiers. There is also an experimental keyless mode for trying it out. Support through the QR codes in the app is optional, always.

No. Password managers — 1Password, KeePass, KeePassXC, Bitwarden, LastPass, Dashlane and Enpass — are blocked by default, so KBMK never listens while you use them. You can block any other app too, and Ctrl+Alt+T pauses KBMK anywhere, instantly.

Because the builds are unsigned — code-signing certificates cost money that a free, independent project does not spend. SmartScreen will warn once: choose More info → Run anyway. On macOS, right-click the app and choose Open the first time.

Yes. Bengali is where KBMK is strongest — it handles Bengali script, including the danda (।), and text typed with Avro Keyboard. In the language menu, searching “bangla” finds বাংলা immediately. One note: DeepL does not offer Bengali, so use a Google or Azure key for it.

Google Cloud Translation for the widest coverage — all 100+ languages. Azure Translator if you prefer Microsoft’s free tier. DeepL for especially natural European languages, keeping in mind its ~35 languages and no Bengali. You can keep several keys and switch any time; every profile has a Test button and its own usage counter.

Only the word or short phrase you finished typing or pasted, sent to the translation provider you chose, with your own key. Nothing else — no telemetry, no analytics, no tracking. Your keystrokes are never written to disk, and your keys never leave Windows Credential Manager.

More than software, KBMK is a bridge — built so every voice can be heard, and every heart can be understood.
